title: Desire to Move Permanently to U.S. at New Low
summary_raw: Article URL: https://news.gallup.com/poll/708614/desire-migrate-drops-new-low.aspx Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50120664 Points: 36 # Comments: 11
fulltext:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. remains the most desired destination for people who would like to leave their own countries permanently, but Gallup's latest data show it is less attractive than it once was.
In 2025, 15% of adults worldwide who say they would like to move permanently to another country name the U.S. as their preferred destination, the lowest level recorded in nearly two decades of Gallup research. From 2007 to 2009, 24% of would-be migrants named the U.S. as their top choice, and that figure remained near 20% through 2016. Since 2017, it has been at or below 18%.
The rank order of the countries attracting the most interest from potential migrants has seen little change since Gallup’s first measure. Canada ranks second, as it has for several years, with 9% of potential migrants mentioning the U.S. neighbor. The appeal of these desired destinations did not change in 2025, even as the U.S. became less desirable.
Line charts show trends in the percentage of adults worldwide who would like to move permanently to top destination countries from 2007–2009 to 2025. The United States remains the top destination but declines from 24% to 15%. Canada rises from 7% to 9%. The United Kingdom declines from 7% to 4%. Germany, Australia, Spain, France, Japan, Italy, and Saudi Arabia remain broadly stable around 3% to 5%.
Gallup's latest update on migration desire is based on a question asked almost annually: “Ideally, if you had the opportunity, would you like to move permanently to another country, or would you prefer to continue living in this country?” Those who say they would like to move are then asked to name their preferred destination.
Results for 2025 are based on interviews with over 144,000 adults in 140 countries. The current estimates include data from China for 2023, the last time the question was asked there.
The most recent analysis period coincides with a sharp slowdown in international migration into the U.S., amid changes in immigration policy and declining migration desire in several regions. External data suggest global migration more broadly slowed in 2024 after surging post-pandemic.
Declining Desire to Move to the U.S.
The U.S. became less attractive to adults in several regions in 2025, with statistically significant declines in Latin America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Latin America accounts for seven of the 16 countries worldwide where the percentage naming the U.S. as a preferred destination fell by at least 10 points. In the region, the percentage fell from 33% in 2024 to 28% in 2025.
Other Latin American countries that saw double-digit declines include U.S. neighbor Mexico, where the latest 21% who want to move to the U.S. matches the previous low set in 2017 and 2018. In Honduras, desire to migrate to the U.S. dropped 35 percentage points, from 71% to 36%, the largest decline in any country in 2025.
Despite the falling numbers, the U.S. remains by far the most desired destination in Latin America and the Caribbean and in sub-Saharan Africa. The picture varies more in other regions.
In Southeast Asia, Japan leads at 23%, compared with 12% for the U.S. In the Middle East and North Africa, Germany attracts 13% and Saudi Arabia 12% of potential migrants, with the U.S. at 9%. In South Asia, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. are roughly tied, each cited by 7%. Within the European Union, Spain, at 11%, and Switzerland, at 8%, rank ahead of the U.S., at 6%.
Global Desire to Migrate Falls, Shifts
Beyond where people want to go, the data also show a shift in how many want to move at all.
Overall, global desire to migrate declined in 2025 to its lowest level in a decade, driven by sharp drops in regions that have long had the highest migration aspirations, including Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa. After holding at a record-high 16% between 2021 and 2024, global desire dipped in 2025 for the first time in years, falling one point to 15%, a level not seen since 2018.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, 25% of adults say they would like to move permanently to another country, the lowest level in a decade. The decline is particularly notable in this region, where migration desire has fallen steadily after peaking at 34% in 2021-2022.
Multiple countries across the region recorded double-digit declines between 2024 and 2025. In Honduras and El Salvador, the percentage of adults wanting to leave fell sharply last year, from levels above 50% in several prior years to 35% and 25%, respectively.
In sub-Saharan Africa, where migration desire remains the highest globally, 33% say they would like to move permanently, also a decade low. As recently as 2023, that figure stood at 37%, ticking upward from 36% in 2021-2022.
In regions that are typically on the receiving end of migrants, the picture is different. Migration desire in the United States and Canada (20%) and the European Union (21%) remains near record highs.
In the U.S., notably, the heightened desire to move abroad is concentrated among women younger than 45. In 2025, 40% of U.S. women aged 15 to 44 say they would move permanently to another country if they had the opportunity, up from 10% in 2014. The trend first rose sharply in 2016 and continued across multiple years, suggesting a broader shift in outlook rather than a short-term political effect.
Bottom Line
It is important to note that desire to migrate is not the same as intent to move. Not everyone who wants to move can or will do so. The 2025 data show that fewer people worldwide are imagining their futures elsewhere, and the U.S., long the world’s most desired destination, is attracting less of that interest than at any point in nearly two decades.
For years, the dominant story in global migration data was a rising desire to move across nearly every region. The 2025 data suggest that pattern is shifting. The declines are widespread and concentrated in the regions that have historically driven global migration.

title: America's Wumao: Inside Polymarket's Paid Quote-Retweet Esports Program
summary_raw: Article URL: https://www.readergrev.com/p/polymarket-paid-quote-retweet-esports-investigation Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50120010 Points: 47 # Comments: 23
fulltext:
Screenshots from X; minor background elements by Sonny Ross
Hiya! Thanks for reading ReaderGrev. ICYMI, consider watching my investigation into threatening letters sent on behalf of Bobby Kotick to publications covering allegations of sexual misconduct and gender-based discrimination at Activision. It’s a doozy.
As I mentioned last week, I’ve launched a paid tier of the newsletter. All the money coming from subscriptions will go toward reporting and publishing, covering costs associated with legal review, public records, web hosting, mail, software subscriptions, business admin, travel, and (silliest of all) buying new games.
My next newsletter (which will be available exclusively to paid subscribers) is going to be a follow-up to this report, going into why I think prediction markets’ growing influence is worth covering and taking a much broader view of the issue, beyond just the reporting. If that sounds interesting, consider upgrading your subscription. I’ll also include some outtakes from this story: reporting that just didn’t make sense for this particular piece.
Lastly, I want to thank Ollie Ring for his help as I was reporting this newsletter. Ollie writes the Lootboxes & Leftovers newsletter on Substack. Check it out. And much love to Riley MacLeod of Aftermath, where this story will be reprinted later today, for editing this piece.
Polymarket, the prediction market platform, is paying social media users to quote-retweet content from its branded esports accounts. The program includes over 800 participants, according to posts by a Polymarket representative in an internal Discord, and offers rates ranging from $10 to several hundred per post, paid in crypto.
Paying social media users to engage with content is not illegal, and the Polymarket program has robust guidelines around disclosure and the kinds of quote retweets the company is looking for. But the slight “Paid partnership” tag on X — a common sight on the app, and the only public indication that there’s money changing hands — belies the scale and sophistication of Polymarket’s esports operation, which has more than doubled in size since August. And all the while, in the Discord, Polymarket representatives have repeatedly reminded participants in the program to write posts in a way that should appear “organic,” in what one expert said was an effort to ingratiate the prediction market with esports fans and casual observers.
“Literally this needs to look organic and if your X profile looks like Polymarket billboard that looks absoutely [sic] awful,” wrote one Polymarket rep in the Discord.
Polymarket offers two products: Polymarket Global, which is inaccessible to bettors in the United States, and Polymarket US, which is subject to U.S. regulations. In esports — a growing market for the company — Polymarket offers lines around the outcomes of major events and matches, player statistics, as well as novelty bets, including some relating to the teams that players might transfer to in the off-season.1
The prediction market company’s esports outreach is something of an open secret in the esports world — with an emphasis on “open.” Some social media users have expressed dismay over the increasing prevalence of gambling and betting-adjacent companies in the esports scene, having previously been burnt by “here today, gone tomorrow” attention from deep-pocketed crypto companies and venture capital firms. But while elements of the paid marketing program have previously been reported, little concrete information has been revealed until now about the logistical apparatus behind it, the costs involved, and the Discord server from which the program is run — even as the payments by Polymarket to creators have inspired speculation and debate among esports fans.
Emails to Polymarket’s official press line seeking comment, as well as direct messages to numerous Polymarket representatives from the Discord seeking interviews, went unanswered.
A list of participants in the Discord includes prominent esports commentators, current and former professional players, team coaches and managers, media entrepreneurs and content creators, PR professionals, amateur roster reporters, employees of esports tournament organizers, and various social media gadflies.
When figures like that quote-retweet posts like the one embedded below with a sentence or two of commentary, they may be receiving tens or even hundreds of dollars in compensation.
Still, many of the posters paid to quote-retweet Polymarket’s content are virtual unknowns, with low four-figure follower counts on X.
Prospective participants in the marketing program are typically contacted via social media or email. If they show interest in continuing the conversation, they’re brought into a Polymarket Discord server. In that server, dedicated channels for individual esport titles ping users about the tweets they should quote-retweet — which generally focus on some ongoing event or storyline, and the corresponding market on which users can bet, which is linked to in the post.
“New tweet is up: Like + QRT. Replies appreciated,” reads a typical message, which includes a link to the tweet. “Text-only quote from your own account. Counts for the next 24 hours only.” These messages used to also include the phrase “+ Paid Partnership tag,” urging users to disclose their participation in the program. That text has not appeared on the Discord prompts since late August, for reasons that were not immediately clear.
Users are concurrently onboarded to a proprietary tool called PolyTrack, a dashboard into which they can input their tax information, crypto wallet address, and eventually, the quote-retweets for which they will be paid. The platform tracks monthly and lifetime earnings, and offers guidance about the kinds of posts that meet the program’s criteria.
While this report is exclusively focused on Polymarket’s promotional efforts on X, PolyTrack also includes the option to input video and streaming platforms.

title: What on Earth Is Dekton?
summary_raw: Article URL: https://www.worksinprogress.news/p/porcelain Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118828 Points: 63 # Comments: 19
fulltext:
This is our fifth article from Issue 26, which arrived with print subscribers last week. In it, Charles C Mann explains how he learned to love porcelain.
I am aware that I am a bit of a kitchen equipment nerd, okay? So maybe you don’t have to roll your eyes theatrically like my cousins did when I tell you my wife and I got a swanky induction cooktop that was, well, kind of pricey for a middle-class couple? And maybe you can imagine my irritation when it turned out that the swanky induction cooktop – did I mention it was pricey? – did not include the necessary smooth cooking surface above the induction burners, and that you had to buy the cooking surface separately from a separate company, a fact not exactly advertised on the website, and that the surface could not be tempered glass, which is what I had thought was on top of induction ranges, a sheet of which costs maybe $30 per square foot, but a special, newly created material called Dekton that cost five times as much. ‘What on earth is Dekton?’ I asked the heavens, or at least my wife.
My question turned out to have two answers. The first is that Dekton is an artificial material invented by the Spanish company Cosentino in 2013 that is amazingly heat-, pressure-, scratch-, shatter-, and stain-resistant – a high-tech substance that would have been almost impossible to fashion even thirty years ago. The other answer, equally true, is that Dekton is basically porcelain.
Paradoxically, porcelain is both one of humankind’s oldest high technologies and one of its newest. The earliest proto-porcelain was created more than three thousand years ago, and was, for the time, an astonishing technical feat, as unprecedented as the roughly concurrent development of iron metallurgy. Iron technology had its second flowering in the mid-nineteenth century, when the invention of the Bessemer and Siemens-Martin refining processes allowed manufacturers to produce cheap, high-quality steel. Porcelain is having its resurgence today – indeed, high-tech ceramics are key elements in the ongoing upsurge in materials science, the study of the relationship between a substance’s structure and its physical properties.
Much attention is rightfully focused now on the rise of the digital world and the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence. But that attention sometimes obscures the ongoing, equally important transformation of our physical world, the built environment, by materials science. Unleashing a cataract of innovation so ubiquitous as to be almost invisible, materials science has literally changed the walls around us. Porcelain is a reminder that the drive to create new types of matter has long played a powerful role in human history.
Kaolin
The initial steps toward porcelain occurred when potters in northern China started to tinker with an unusual clay, chalk colored and fine grained, called kaolin. Kaolin was known for its color, useful in paints, coatings, and fillers. Potters learned that subjecting this soft, white, unremarkable-looking mud to extreme temperatures produced startling effects.
Ordinary clay looks like amorphous glop but actually is composed of huge numbers of microscopic crystals. The crystals have an unusual structure: flat plates stacked atop each other like playing cards in a deck, loosely held together by hydroxyl groups (hydrogen and oxygen bound together, or -OH, in chemists’ terms). When clay is cooked in a kiln, the hydroxyl groups vibrate and break free, causing the plates to fall apart and reform into long, needle-shaped crystals that lock together into a sturdy structure. Meanwhile, the free hydroxyls merge, becoming water molecules that steam away in the hot kiln, leaving behind oxygen in the new crystals.
Kaolin clay is abundant in kaolinite, a mineral made of aluminum, silicon, oxygen, and hydrogen – Al2Si2O5(OH)4, with the parentheses meaning that each molecule has four hydroxyl groups. When heated in a kiln, kaolinite also loses its hydroxyls and reorganizes itself into a three-dimensional web of needle-like crystals. But when the temperature rises to about 1,200 degrees centigrade, well above the typical level for earthenware pottery, kaolin does something else. The silicon and oxygen break free, forming silica, which forms a thick liquid glass, filling all the spaces around and inside the web of needles, creating a dense, continuous, translucent matrix – porcelain.
In China, like everywhere else, ceramics had been a foundational industry for millennia. Clay was a primary part of construction (bricks, adobe, wattle-and-daub), cooking (pots, tableware), art (paints as well as sculpture), and even communication – clay tablets were the first surfaces used for writing. But porcelain was a giant leap, a concatenation of multiple innovations.
Ordinary kilns couldn’t reach the temperatures required to fire porcelain, partly because their exhaust vents, located on the ‘roof’, let out the hot air almost as fast as it was created, cooling the kiln. (This is a problem for conventional home fireplaces, which are fun to look at in use but wildly inefficient as a means of heating.) Chinese potters designed downdrafts, which forced the hot air to escape through floor vents, trapping the heat around the pottery. Alarmingly, ordinary kilns would shatter or even melt at such high temperatures. Chinese potters invented new types of heat-resistant brick. And so on.
Alltinktur
When Europeans first saw East Asian porcelain, probably in the thirteenth century, they were astounded. Harder, stronger, finer, smoother, and more lustrous than any other pottery, it became an obsessive object of desire, ‘white gold’ for the Continent’s wealthy and powerful. Enormous sets of gleaming white china became symbols of luxury – the private jets and invite-only clubs of the Renaissance era.
Unhappy about the high prices charged by the merchants who imported porcelain from Asia, European elites spent lavishly on efforts to make their own porcelain – and fail

title: How to Formalize All of Mathematics
summary_raw: Article URL: https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/10/16/how-to-formalize-all-of-mathematics/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118512 Points: 46 # Comments: 42
fulltext:
(This is a guest post, written by Jeremy Avigad, Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin, Rémy Degenne, Kim Morrison, Oliver Nash and Adam Topaz.)
Mathematicians’ reactions to last week’s big OpenAI release range from excitement to frustration, but one thing is clear: AI has become remarkably good at proving theorems, both formally and informally. The successes in the formal realm have led AI enthusiasts to declare that now is the time to formalize all of mathematics as a legacy for future generations.
We are sympathetic to this proposal. We recognize the power of new technologies for mathematical reasoning and appreciate what they can contribute to the subject we know and love. We are generally optimistic about the role AI can play, but we are deeply concerned by some recent calls to formalize everything as quickly as possible. If done well, a large-scale, coordinated formalization effort could enormously expand mathematical exploration and discovery. Done poorly, it will be, at best, a waste of resources; more likely, it will do lasting damage.
We prefer to see formalization done well. This post therefore clarifies our concerns, describes some of our experiences with AI and formalization, and offers a positive vision of how we can all work toward a world in which all, or almost all, mathematical definitions, theorems, and proofs are equipped with a formal representation, and in which these artifacts help mathematics flourish.
Just as the role of AI in mathematics is a fraught subject these days, so too is its role in formalization. The range of attitudes among expert formalizers toward AI is as wide as the range of attitudes among mathematicians more broadly. We are aware that some of our closest friends and colleagues, whose opinions we value and respect highly, stand strongly opposed to large-scale formalization using AI. Nothing we say here should be taken as representative of the views of any of the organizations or communities with which we are associated.
The concerns
Let’s start with the observation that a formal artifact is not worth much if nobody uses it. When Math, Inc. tried to hijack a project to formalize Maryna Viazovska’s higher-dimensional sphere-packing results last February, it impressively demonstrated what the technology could do, but beyond that, it contributed nothing to mathematics. The original project team kept preparing a quality formalization of the 8-dimensional result and soon discovered that cleaning up the AI-generated code was more trouble than it was worth; it turned out it was better to throw the code away and do it right, still with ample help from AI.
When Anthropic announced that Claude had formally verified Fermat’s Last Theorem with 13 million lines of code written over 11 days, Kevin Buzzard cheerfully lauded the result while also declaring he had no intention of ending his ongoing formalization of a more modern proof. Once again, although the accomplishment is impressive, this piece of AI-generated code probably has little ongoing value.
What is going on here? The theorems were not seriously in doubt, so the value of the formal artifacts lies solely in what we get beyond mere correctness. We want to formalize everything because we want to use the formalizations to do more mathematics, and to do it better than we could have done without them. We want to think about possible generalizations, explore connections between different branches of mathematics, and consider unexpected applications. We want to refactor and improve our knowledge: part of the joy of manual formalization comes from realizing that we can adjust our concepts to make them more elegant, more efficient, and better suited to our purposes. Knowledge isn’t worth having until it contributes to our understanding; the value of a formalization comes from our ability to use and interact with the data.
When OpenAI announced solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations that blow up in finite time, the natural-language proof was accompanied by a Lean formalization. In contrast to the previous examples, the correctness signal played a key role here: there seems to be little doubt now that the solution is correct, even though the natural-language proof is mostly incomprehensible. OpenAI nonetheless drew the mathematics community’s anger over concerns about how it obtained the result, provenance and credit for ideas, and worries that focusing on correctness alone discouraged the exploration and understanding the Millenium prize was meant to foster. So, even here, the unadorned formal artifact is a mixed blessing. OpenAI’s later dump contains astonishing and important mathematics, and at the same time shows a remarkable disregard for readers and for building understanding (some results have been retracted, many of the informal/formal pairs diverge in subtle or significant ways, and most of the informal writeups are impenetrable).
This explains our concern. If spending millions of dollars to formalize mathematics results in libraries nobody uses, it will be a terrible waste of resources. Worse, the project could disincentivize good research and productive use of AI, disrupt the social norms and practices research depends on, and set the field back decades. A grand failure will make it hard, or even impossible, to recover later. A lousy formalization of existing results is worse than no formalization at all.
The positives
Some of the results from the big labs have been done well: OpenAI’s unit distance conjecture work, and Anthropic’s work on the density of Riemann zeta zeroes stand out. They demonstrated impressive new capabilities, contributed to understanding, and the community subsequently built on their work. These are examples of how the labs can contribute positively and we invite further constructive partnerships between the research community and the labs.
Good formal libraries will enable the positive vision we have for the future of mathematical research. Humans, AIs, and the Lean language work in c

summary_raw: Article URL: https://anuragbhatia.com/post/2026/06/rfc8950-announce-ipv4-with-ipv6-next-hop/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50118267 Points: 44 # Comments: 16
fulltext:
RFC8950: Announce IPv4 with an IPv6 next-hop
For the last few days I have been playing with RFC8950 setup, which allows routing of IPv4 on top of IPv6. While logically it’s quite simple, it has a very powerful application towards making “IPv4 an optional” feature riding on top of an IPv6 network (but without any tunnels!)
Some of the interesting use cases:
- A large network can run IPv6 only everywhere on its core and leave IPv4 only on edge devices. This can work without customers doing any tweaking at their end. They still do things the old way but Backbone can run IPv6 only at its core.
- An IP transit backbone can run IPv6 only while exchanging IPv4 routes with its customers/peers/upstream over IPv6 sessions. So IPv4 as a “feature” stays but the network in itself is IPv6 only without the overhead of IPv4 interface config, BGP session config, firewall config, etc.
- An IXP can offer services without IPv4 essentually by using a (unique) IPv6 at the IX LAN & running route server to exchange both IPv4 & IPv6 routes over the IPv6 only session.
Thus what 464XLAT did to the mobile networks - this has the potential to do that for the backbone networks.
How does it work?
Multi-protocol BGP (MP-BGP) supports announcement of IPv4 routes over IPv6 sessions with IPv4 next-hops and IPv6 routes over IPv4 sessions with IPv6 next-hops. RFC8950 extends this feature for IPv4 to have IPv6 next-hops. So for IPv4 address, next hop is IPv6, IPv6 reach works via usual NDP and IPv4 rides on ethernet frames to the same MAC as discovered by the NDP. Technically RFC8950 only impacts control plane decisions by using IPv6 as the control plane but keeps the data plane as it is. IPv4 stays IPv4 & goes as IPv4 over the wire unlike say some tunnel or 464xLAT etc.
Hardware support
As of now it’s quite widely supported by a lot of routing platforms like Juniper JunOS, Cisco IOS XR, Nokia SR OS, Mikrotik, Huawei, BIRD, FRR etc. So, it is very likely supported if you are running a recent version of the OS.
Demo lab
Here’s a fun lab with two customer routers: C1 & C2 connected via provider routers R1-R2-R3 in Container Lab. All routers here are running open source FRR.
- C1 is IPv6 only on the WAN side facing R1. It originates 10.0.0.0/24 to R1 over an IPv6 session.
- R1 & R2 are IPv6 only with no IPv4 anywhere on their interfaces (but carry IPv4 routes in their table)
- R3 has IPv6 with R2 but just IPv4 only with C2. So C2 is like a typical enterprise user who lacks IPv6 deployment and still wants IPv4 only to work.
- R3 has 100.64.0.0/24 and originates it in the IPv4 table (to IPv6 adjacency - R2)
- C2 sits on 100.64.0.2/30 given by R3 and communicate in IPv4 only.
- C1 and C2 can reach each other over this network with parts being IPv6 only without any tunnel.

title: Bark: The Toll-Free BBS for 90s Teens
summary_raw: Article URL: https://blog.bityard.net/articles/2026/October/bark-the-toll-free-bbs-for-90s-teens Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50117504 Points: 30 # Comments: 9
fulltext:
Topics: Retrocomputing
The other day I was thinking about the first communities I found online and, perhaps tangentially, to what degree they influenced the amount of therapy I now require to function normally as an adult. Our family's second computer came from Sam's Club. It was a 386DX with Windows 3.0 but my inner nerd would have nothing to do with cheerful bit-mapped color schemes, preferring instead to exit to MS-DOS and do all necessary computing and gaming from a command prompt and text-based GUIs. Hardware-wise, it looked and felt cheap. The machine was less reliable than the cardboard box it came in. It was a Packard Bell and if you were to read this paragraph to anyone who was into computers in the 1990's, they will hear that name and then simply close their eyes and nod quietly in sympathetic understanding.
(Nostalgic Modem Noises)
Most importantly, it came with a dial-up modem. My mom's series of reactions when I told her I had plugged our new computer into the telephone line were as follows:
- "Huh, you can do that?"
- "But why would you do that?"
- "WHAT HAVE YOU DONE AND HOW MUCH DO WE OWE?!"
Now in my defense, as a semi-rebellious teenager eager to experience literally anything outside languid rural Midwest life, I often leaned hard into the practice of begging forgiveness in lieu of asking permission. Sometimes I even got away with it.
To give a better idea of the timeline and circumstances, the Internet as we know today it only kind of existed in the early 90's. There was email, there were message boards, file exchange programs, remote login to other systems, real-time chat (IRC) and so on. The web was new and promising and free of ads but not at all the main attraction just yet. And unless you lived in a city or attended a university with a well-funded technology department, the Internet was probably not yet accessible to you. Or for the purposes of this article, me.
But bulletin board systems (BBSes) had been around since at least the early 80's. Maybe earlier, I'm not sure. These were computers connected to phone lines. When you called a number with your computer, the other computer answered, and you could interact with whatever software the sysop (system operator) had set up. Usually these contained at least public and private message boards, but many also had places where you could download and upload files, chat in real time with others (if the BBS had multiple lines), or play games.
How I came upon the early essentials necessary to connect our computer to other computers is a complete mystery to me at this point. I didn't know anyone else with a modem and my school's computer situation was about a decade behind: "computer" classes were really typing classes taught by a cartoon cat named PAWS on Apple IIs. Back at home, at a bare minimum, I would have needed a terminal program to dial up and interact with another computer. So did I have one already or did I grab one off a shareware floppy that came in some magazine? Where did I even find the number of the first BBS (bulletin-board system) to call?
What happened next is easier to remember. I racked up quite the collection of informative text files from that first handful of BBSes I found, which generally included programming guides, hacking e-zines (Phrack!), some anarchy-type content, and rather entertaining but unhinged conspiracy theories. And of course, where to find more BBSes. I also clearly remember downloading as much software as I could get my hands on. Plenty of development tools, different modem terminal programs, and scads of DOS utilities. I learned a lot in a very short amount of time about BBS software, doors, Kermit, X/Y/Zmodem and ZIP files. It took about two hours to download enough data to fill up a 1.44MB floppy disk over a 2400 baud modem. (Eventually I managed to con my mom into buying a 14.4kbps modem a little bit later. I still have no idea how. Maybe because we had a free trial of Prodigy and that needed a faster modem to draw all the fancy vector graphics?)
But that all came to a swift end when my mom got the phone bill at the end of the month. In those days, local calls were free, long distance calls cost money. You paid by the minute and it was not especially cheap. The problem was, we lived in a town so small you could just about trip over it on your way to somewhere interesting, so everything outside a 1.5-mile radius was long distance. I never heard what the monetary damage was, but she did state in no uncertain terms that it would not be allowed to happen again.
1-800-YOU-NERD
(Don't actually call this, I don't know where it goes.)
One of the files I happened to grab was a list of toll-free BBSes. Or as we'd say back before more toll-free codes were added, "1-800 numbers." I didn't know exactly what I would find at these numbers, but that was a big part of the appeal. The first list I downloaded was TB01-94.TXT by Doug Schneider. Here are some others that I have in my collection from around that time frame:
- TB06-96.TXT - Newer version of "The Best 800 List", also in in the wayback machine. (Click on the ZIP, not the TXT.)
- ECBALAM.TXT - "1-800- BBS'S ACROSS THE US" by Bryan Balam - Date Unknown
- BBSWORK3.TXT - "BBS's That Actually Work!" by Kevin Ardoin - August 1994
- BBSWOR41.TXT - "BBS's That Actually Work!" by Kevin Ardoin - December 1994
- TRANSBBS.TXT - "TRANSPORTATION-RELATED ELECTRONIC BULLETIN BOARD SYSTEMS (BBS)"
I have a very clear memory of trying numbers in some semi-random order, crossing off the ones that never answered and highlighting interesting ones to come back to later. I wrote notes next to some. The crossed-off lines outnumbered the highlighted lines 10-to-1 at least. If I ran into a busy signal, it would sometimes be quite a while before I came back to it. It turned out that these toll-free computer systems came and went faster than people could update and pass around the text files. The vast majority of the numbers I called responded with any of:
- Endles

title: The Folders Programming Language
summary_raw: Article URL: https://danieltemkin.com/esolangs/folders Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50114342 Points: 178 # Comments: 31
fulltext:
The Folders Language
Created 2015 | Updated 2026 | One of Forty-Four Esolangs, by the creator of Rivulet and Velato
Where directories are code and drive space is infinite
About
Folders is a non-textual language, where code is expressed in containment and order alone. The names of the folders are ignored, apart from alphabetical ordering. In other words, they are pure ordered trees.
Inspired by the Whitespace language, Folders is devoted to the idea of dematerialized code. It began with the question What is more empty than a file with no visible text? The empty folder is clutter, an appendage with no purpose. In git, it is ignored entirely (for this reason, it is suggested that Folders programs put .gitignore files in their deepest reaches).
Folders began as a Windows language. In Windows, folders are an even more extreme measure of emptiness: they take up no disk space at all. For proof, create 352,449 folders and get properties on it. In this way, Folders offers not only a dematerialized approach to code but also infinite storage capacity. Keep all your data encoded in folder names and never worry about running out of space again.
For those who use other operating systems, the emulator below gives some of the experience of how Folders manages data and code.
The original implementation can be found on github.
Encoding
Each command folder has at least one child folder. The number of subfolders in the first folder (alphabetically) indicates the type of command; any arguments are indicated in a second folder; some commands require a third folder. Expressions are the same: the number of folders in the first sub-folder determine what kind of expression it is. The full Language Spec is below.
Temporary data is stored as folders; unlike Folders code, it is the name of the folder that stores the data.
Folders FS
The Folders interpreter does not create temp files; anything not held immediately in memory is stored as a set of temp folders. Unlike Folders code, the name of the folder stores the data itself. The prefered I/O of Folders is another set of folders. This means you can encode all your data in folders, bypassing the "material realm" of files entirely and giving you infinite disk space (attempt at your own risk). Folders lang for code, Folders FS for data storage.
Visualizations
A Folders program is a nil-terminated nested list. Its simplest form is pure containment and order, like this all-array JSON:
That is also how the JS emulator saves/reads Folders programs.
However, other systems of visualization are possible. Folders programs are content as structure and can be applied to raw data of any type. Here is a Truth Machine as a contour map. The thicker lines are containers, and the order of folders is read starting at the upper left (NW corner) and proceeding counter-clockwise.
Other visualizations might be a family tree (with all single parents), a botanical branching structure (like a splitting stalk of wheat), or the paths through a maze.
The red dots indicate a threshhold from a container to a single child.
Language Spec
The language itself is a very simple imperative language with a short list of semantic rules.
For Commands and Expressions, the number of folders in their first child folder determines their use. Types are used directly.
Commands
| Command | # of Folders | Details | 
|---|---|---|
| if | 0 folders | Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands | 
| while | 1 folder | Second sub-folder holds expression, third holds list of commands | 
| declare | 2 folders | Second sub-folder holds type, third holds var name (in number of folders) | 
| let | 3 folders | Second holds var name (in number of folders), third holds expression | 
|  | 4 folders | Second sub-folder holds expression | 
| input | 5 folders | Second sub-folder holds var name | 
Expressions
| Type | # of Folders | Details | 
|---|---|---|
| variable | 0 folders | Second sub-folder holds var name | 
| add | 1 folder | Second sub-folder holds first expression to add, third holds second expression | 
| subtract | 2 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to subtract, third holds second expression | 
| multiply | 3 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to multiply, third holds second expression | 
| divide | 4 folders | Second sub-folder holds first expression to divide, third holds second expression | 
| literal value | 5 folders | Second sub-folder holds the type of the value (e.g. two folders for a string, third holds the value) | 
| equal to | 6 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
| greater than | 7 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
| less than | 8 folders | Second and third folders hold expressions to compare | 
Types
| Type | # of Folders | 
|---|---|
| float | 1 folder | 
| string | 2 folders | 
| char | 3 folders |
